newsitem.title: INDIA: U.N. chief backs bilateral Indo-Pakistani talks.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief backs bilateral Indo-Pakistani talks.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Monday threw his support behind peace talks between India and Pakistan, saying a 49-year-old U.N. resolution calling for a referendum had failed to solve their dispute over Kashmir.
Annan endorsed high-level bilateral talks that resumed last month, and urged the long time rivals to tackle disagreements step-by-step, leaving aside more contentious issues for later.
That approach has been pushed by India, which is willing to put aside the half-century dispute over the Himalayan region of Kashmir and reach agreements in other, less thorny areas.

But Pakistan, which rules one third of the region, considers Kashmir to be the "core issue" in the talks, and wants a U.N.-sponsored plebescite of Kashmiris to determine if the area is folded into Islamic Pakistan or mostly Hindu India.
The dispute has been pending at the U.N. since 1948, shortly after India and Pakistan fought the first of their three wars.

India says the Kashmir dispute should be discussed under a 1972 agreement between the two neighbours, while Pakistan says the pact does not preclude a U.N.-sponsored referendum cited in a 1948 U.N. Security Council resolution.
"I am very pleased that high-level talks are going on between India and Pakistan," Annan told a news conference at the end of a three-day visit to the Indian capital.

The U.N. chief said he had talked to both Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and his Pakistani counterpart, Gohar Ayub Khan, while in New Delhi, where Annan and Khan were attending a meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement.
"We will do whatever we can to support it (talks), but I think the way they are approaching it is the best, in that there are direct talks going on," he said.
Annan urged India and Pakistan to make progress in areas such as movement of people, visas, trade and communication.
The U.N. chief was asked if he would urge the two countries to put aside the Kashmir issue and concentrate on other issues.

"I would put it in the terms that when you start solving a problem that is complex and a problem of many parts, there are certain elements that you can deal with fairly quickly, which you can solve and make progress and move on and build good will.

"What I am suggesting is we should move ahead and resolve those issues we can to build good will, and in time resolve all the issues. You do not refuse to move ahead because you cannot resolve the most difficult issue or a difficult issue."
He was asked if U.N. resolutions, among them the one calling for an internationally supervised plebescite, could be the basis for a resolution of differences between the two nations.

"Obviously they (resolutions) have not solved the problem after all these years. The two governments are now talking directly and taking steps in their own way to resolve it, and I think that is the right way to go," he said.

The foreign secretaries of India and Pakistan agreed last month to hold a second round of talks in Islamabad but did not set dates, partly because of the political crisis threatening Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.

The two nations' foreign ministers were scheduled to hold talks over breakfast on Wednesday. Diplomats said the discussion was likely to be brief as Deve Gowda faces a vote of confidence in parliament on Friday.
